## Critique

Many of the colleague's hypotheses rest on loose "synergy vs. saturation" stories that could go either way. In NAS-Bench-201 the strongest and most reliable interactions are **structural**: an edit has almost no effect when the edited edge cannot carry signal to the output. That happens when its source node gets no input, or when its target node has no path onward.

**Kept (13):** #1, #2, #5, #7, #8, #10, #11, #12, #14, #15, #17, #18, #20.
- The skip-redundancy and shallow-collapse claims (#7, #8, #11) match the known NB201 pattern.
- The residual-plus-deep-conv claim (#10) does too.
- The substitution and buffering claims (#5, #14, #17) are plausible.

**Dropped and replaced (7):**
- **#3 (e2 conv | e0 conv, higher):** the direction is genuinely ambiguous. Replaced with **e2 conv | e0 none, lower**. With node 1 empty, edge 2 carries zero signal, so the upgrade does nothing.
- **#4 (e2 conv | e0 pool, lower):** a weak effect. Replaced with **e2 conv | e5 none, lower**. Node 2 is then a dead end, so the edit is inert.
- **#6 (e1 none | e2 pool, lower):** a marginal effect. Replaced with **e1 none | e5 none, higher**. Cutting an edge into a dead-end node costs nothing.
- **#9 (e4 skip | e5 conv, higher):** the dilution and gradient-flow arguments cancel out. Replaced with **e3 skip | e3 none, higher**. Adding the missing residual gains far more than swapping out a conv.
- **#13 (e0 conv | e4 pool, lower):** a weak effect. Replaced with **e0 conv | e4 none, lower**. Node 1's only route to the output is then the edge 2→5 path.
- **#16 (e1 conv | e2 skip, higher):** ambiguous. Replaced with **e1 conv | e5 none, lower**, because node 2 is disconnected from the output.
- **#19 (e5 1x1 | e4 conv3, lower):** weak and noisy. Replaced with **e4 conv | e0 none, lower**. Edge 4 then reads an empty node.
